p: Francis Bacon, Lord Chancellor of England under King James the First, and a philosopher of greater merit than his honesty, wrote that three inventions had changed the whole face and state of things throughout the world: printing, gunpowder and the compass, the first in literature, the second in warfare, the third in navigation. He did not know, or did not trouble to say, that all three came first from China. But of the three, I think printing has done the most, and it is the one to which a man in my trade owes everything.

Before printing, every book in Europe was written by hand. A skilled scribe, working in good light, might copy a few pages a day; a large Bible might take a year or more. Books were therefore precious, rare and expensive, chained to the desks of libraries, and owned chiefly by churches, monasteries, universities and the very rich. Every copy introduced new errors, and copies of copies grew progressively more corrupt, so that scholars of the same text might be reading quite different words. A great library of the fourteenth century, such as that of the Sorbonne in Paris, might contain some two thousand volumes. I have more than that in my own house, and I am not a rich man. That is the measure of the change.

Printing from carved wooden blocks was practised in China by the seventh or eighth century. The oldest printed book with a date that survives is a copy of a Buddhist scripture, the Diamond Sutra, printed in the year eight hundred and sixty-eight and found in the cave temples of Dunhuang; it was carried to London by a Hungarian-British explorer named Aurel Stein in nineteen hundred and seven, and is in the British Library. About the year ten forty, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng made movable type of baked clay, each character on its own small block, which could be arranged and rearranged. In Korea, printing from movable metal type was practised in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, before it was known in Europe. But Chinese writing, with its thousands of characters, made movable type laborious, and block printing remained more usual there. An alphabet of a few dozen letters was far better suited to it.

The man to whom Europe owes the press was Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith of Mainz, on the Rhine. About the year fourteen forty, while living in Strasbourg, and then in Mainz in the fourteen-fifties, he brought together several inventions into a system. The first was a method of casting individual letters in metal, quickly, precisely and in great numbers, using a hand mould into which an alloy of lead, tin and antimony was poured; the letters were all of exactly the same height, so that they printed evenly. The second was an ink based on oil, like the paints of the Flemish painters, which would cling to metal. The third was the press itself, adapted from the screw presses used to make wine and paper. Together, these allowed a page of type to be set, inked and printed hundreds of times, then broken up and the letters used again.

His great work, the Bible in Latin, printed about fourteen fifty-five, in two large volumes, is one of the most beautiful books ever made; some one hundred and eighty copies were printed, and about forty-nine survive, wholly or in part. Gutenberg himself made little profit; he was sued by his financial partner, Johann Fust, and lost his workshop and much of his equipment. Such is the reward of genius in commercial matters.

The new art spread with a speed that astonished contemporaries. By fifteen hundred, presses had been established in some two hundred and fifty towns of Europe, and they had printed, by the Encyclopaedia's estimate, more than twenty million copies of books. Venice became the greatest centre of printing, where the scholar-printer Aldus Manutius published the Greek and Latin classics in small, cheap volumes that a student could carry in his pocket. William Caxton, a merchant of Kent who had learned the craft in Bruges, set up the first press in England at Westminster in fourteen seventy-six, and printed, among much else, the Canterbury Tales of Chaucer and the Morte d'Arthur of Sir Thomas Malory, a title in French meaning the death of Arthur.

The consequences were incalculable, and I shall name only a few. Texts became fixed: every copy of an edition was the same, and scholars in different cities could refer to the same page. Errors could be corrected in a new edition and stay corrected. Knowledge became cumulative in a way it had never been. The scientific revolution of the following centuries depended utterly on the ability of men like Copernicus, Galileo and Newton to publish their work in hundreds of identical copies, with accurate diagrams and tables, to readers across Europe.

Ideas could now spread faster than authorities could suppress them. When Martin Luther published his protest against the sale of indulgences in fifteen seventeen, it was printed and reprinted across Germany within weeks; within a few years, his writings had sold in hundreds of thousands. Without the press, there would have been no Reformation, or at least not that one. The governments and churches of Europe responded with censorship, licensing and lists of forbidden books, and the struggle between the press and the censor has continued ever since, in my own century and, I am told, in the next.

Printing also encouraged the use of the common tongues of each nation, for there was a market for books in English, French and German far larger than for books in Latin. It helped to fix the spelling and grammar of those languages, though in the case of English, with less success than one could wish. And by making books cheap, it made reading worth learning, and so, slowly, over centuries, it spread literacy from the clergy and the gentry to the people at large. The men of the future, I see, have something they call the internet, which they compare to the press. I shall come to it in its place. I will say only that every one of its enthusiasts should first be made to read the history of what followed Gutenberg, the hundred years of religious war included.
